Q: What is an Intermediate distribution frame (IDF)?
Option1: The building's primary demarcation point for external circuits
Option2: A floor- or area-level wiring closet that aggregates access-layer cabling and uplinks to the building backbone
Option3: A rack-mounted battery backup unit
Option4: A cabinet used only for fiber splicing

Q: What is a Main distribution frame (MDF)?
Option1: The central point in a building or campus where backbone cabling and external circuits terminate
Option2: A closet on each floor for access switches
Option3: A patch panel used for voice only
Option4: A dedicated rack for wireless controllers

Q: How do the MDF and IDFs typically connect?
Option1: IDFs uplink to the MDF over backbone cabling; the MDF is the central hub
Option2: The MDF uplinks to IDFs using short patch cords only
Option3: IDFs connect to the MDF only via wireless bridges
Option4: They are the same element with different names

Q: In a multi-story office, where should the core router and provider handoff usually reside?
Option1: In any floor's IDF
Option2: In the Main distribution frame (MDF)
Option3: On the roof near antennas
Option4: Inside a user cubicle

Q: What does 'rack size' most commonly describe?
Option1: The number of servers allowed by license
Option2: The standardized 19-inch rack width and height measured in rack units (U)
Option3: The weight of the rack in kilograms
Option4: The number of power outlets on the rack

Q: What does a '42U rack' indicate?
Option1: Forty-two outlets on the power strip
Option2: A rack 42 inches wide
Option3: Height capacity of forty-two rack units (each 1U ≈ 1.75 inches)
Option4: A rack rated for 42 kilowatts

Q: What does 'port-side exhaust/intake' refer to?
Option1: The direction of network traffic through the ports
Option2: The orientation of device airflow relative to the port side, used to align with hot/cold aisles
Option3: The number of fan trays in a chassis
Option4: Which side has cable management

Q: If switches have port-side intake, which way should the port side face in hot/cold aisles?
Option1: Toward the hot aisle for cooler air
Option2: Toward the cold aisle to draw in chilled air
Option3: Sideways to the aisle
Option4: It does not matter

Q: What is a patch panel?
Option1: A device that converts alternating current to direct current
Option2: A passive termination panel that organizes copper cabling and allows flexible patching to switch ports
Option3: A wireless controller
Option4: A battery charger

Q: What is a fiber distribution panel?
Option1: A panel for distributing electrical power
Option2: A passive enclosure that protects fiber terminations/splices and presents connectors for patching
Option3: A load balancer for fiber links
Option4: A device that measures optical power only

Q: Why use a patch panel instead of punching horizontal runs directly into a switch?
Option1: It increases the speed of the switch
Option2: It protects switch ports, simplifies changes, and maintains structured cabling
Option3: It provides battery backup for the switch
Option4: It eliminates the need for labeling

Q: What does 'lockable' indicate for racks or closets?
Option1: They are waterproof
Option2: They can be physically secured to restrict access and prevent tampering
Option3: They support only fiber
Option4: They require no ventilation

Q: An open closet suffers from unauthorized cable unplugging. What control best addresses this?
Option1: Use wider wireless channels
Option2: Install a lockable rack or cabinet and enforce access control
Option3: Lower the switch duplex setting
Option4: Disable the captive portal

Q: What is an Uninterruptible power supply (UPS)?
Option1: A rack power strip
Option2: A device that provides temporary battery power and power conditioning during outages or sags
Option3: A generator that supplies power for days
Option4: A device that distributes network VLANs

Q: What is a Power distribution unit (PDU)?
Option1: A battery that keeps devices online during an outage
Option2: A device that distributes electrical power to multiple outlets within a rack; may provide metering or switching
Option3: A fiber optic patch panel
Option4: A voltage regulator for alternating current only

Q: Which pairing is correct regarding rack power?
Option1: UPS provides outlets; PDU provides backup power
Option2: UPS provides backup power; PDU distributes outlets in the rack
Option3: Both provide long-term power like a generator
Option4: Neither is used in racks

Q: What is 'power load' when planning rack power?
Option1: The number of devices in a rack
Option2: The total electrical demand of connected devices, used to size circuits and UPS capacity
Option3: The airflow produced by fans
Option4: The weight of mounted equipment

Q: What does 'voltage' refer to in this context?
Option1: The type of copper cabling in use
Option2: The electrical potential of the supply (for example, 120/208/240 volts) that equipment must support
Option3: The heat output of a rack
Option4: The bandwidth of a link

Q: Your equipment draws 900 watts but the installed UPS is rated for 600 watts. What is the risk?
Option1: Nothing—runtime just increases
Option2: The UPS will be overloaded and may shut down or fail; choose a higher-capacity model
Option3: Only the PDU will fail
Option4: Voltage will automatically increase to compensate

Q: You need per-outlet metering and the ability to reboot specific devices remotely in a rack. Which device meets this need?
Option1: Basic power strip
Option2: Metered or switched Power distribution unit
Option3: Uninterruptible power supply
Option4: Fiber distribution panel

Q: What is the primary concern with humidity in network spaces?
Option1: Humidity has no effect on electronics
Option2: Too low increases electrostatic discharge risk; too high promotes condensation and corrosion
Option3: Only very high humidity is harmful
Option4: Only very low humidity is harmful

Q: What does 'fire suppression' in equipment rooms typically imply?
Option1: Using only water sprinklers above racks
Option2: Using appropriate detection and clean-agent suppression systems designed to protect electronics and people
Option3: Turning off all power to avoid sparks
Option4: Placing fire extinguishers outside the building only

Q: Why is temperature control critical for network installations?
Option1: It prevents wireless interference
Option2: It keeps devices within supported operating ranges and avoids thermal throttling or failure
Option3: It increases link speed
Option4: It eliminates the need for airflow planning

Q: How should airflow orientation align with a hot-aisle/cold-aisle layout?
Option1: Port-side intake should face the hot aisle
Option2: Align device intake with the cold aisle and exhaust with the hot aisle
Option3: Orientation is irrelevant if voltage is correct
Option4: Always exhaust toward the cold aisle for comfort

Q: After adding high-power access switches, the wiring closet overheats. What is the best immediate action?
Option1: Disable encryption on switches
Option2: Increase cooling and ensure clear front-to-back airflow; separate hot and cold aisles
Option3: Lower all interface speeds to 10 megabits per second
Option4: Replace copper with fiber

Q: A basement IDF shows corrosion and occasional condensation. What should be addressed first?
Option1: Increase channel width on the access points
Option2: Control humidity with dehumidification and sealing; maintain recommended environmental range
Option3: Lower rack unit height
Option4: Install a larger Power distribution unit
